toc.title: How the loss shapes the state

blocks.p: How does grief fit into the Polyvagal Theory? Where does it fall on the [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system)? The short answer: everywhere. It's up and down the ladder.

There's a book called Clinical Applications of the Polyvagal Theory. It's a collection of essays from different professions. There's an essay from Deb Dana about therapy and the Polyvagal Theory, and one from her about her husband in a hospital and all the danger cues in there. There are essays on nursing, and I think one on teaching.

One person wrote about grief. I forget her name, but it's one of the essays that really stuck out to me. She lays out that grief is not just that you miss somebody. It's a fundamental change in potentially every aspect of your daily life, depending on circumstances.

I remember she wrote about expecting to say something to that person the next day, realizing they weren't there, and feeling flight/fight kind of stuff. But then at the funeral, there might be a very deep shutdown. Or maybe at first it's more of a freeze, a shock reaction. It could be any of these at any moment. It's all over the polyvagal ladder.

blocks.h: How the loss shapes the state

blocks.p: The context of how you lost somebody is going to play into whether it's more of a freeze or more of a shutdown. If you lose somebody unexpectedly, untimely, or in a brutal kind of death, there's probably going to be more of a shock/freeze factor to it. Compare that with knowing someone is going to pass away, having a chance to say goodbye, and then they pass. Of course that's still going to affect anybody. But it may not be a freeze, or not the same kind of freeze, as someone suddenly being gone in a very brutal way.
The states can show up like this:

ul: Fight: anger at the fact that they're not here anymore.
Flight or freeze: anxiousness. What's life going to be like tomorrow? Can I rely on people to be in my life the next day? There might even be some panicky freeze flavor in there.

blocks.p: When I work with people going through grief, they'll tell me about the painful stuff: how much they miss the person, how things aren't the same, how they're still in shock. But as they share, they'll eventually, naturally, pendulate to a safety anchor. It'll be a memory: "There was this one time they did..." fill in the blank. They'll sit with that for a little while. Then they'll come back to the pain. Then back to a safety anchor: a memory, a certain moment, a laugh.

So it's normal to be up and down the polyvagal ladder: in safety, and also dropping down to really experience shutdown, or anger, or anxiousness. With grief, it's very common to be up and down the ladder.

Story follows state shows up in grief too. When someone is sharing their sadness with me, their story follows their state. They'll be in a shutdown state, feeling deep sadness and maybe numbness, and the story might be how lonely they are, how life doesn't mean anything anymore, how they can't imagine their future. There's no hope, no happiness, nothing. The story might be, "What's the point of living?" or "I cannot continue without this person."
That's the story following the state.

Then, as they process and talk and go through the grieving process, eventually they get to a point where they have appreciation for what they did get to experience. The story becomes that one memory, that one hug, or the overall theme: "I got to live with this person. I got to have them in my life, and wow, am I lucky." That's a story following the state of safety.
Deb Dana put it simply when I interviewed her:

q: You can see how the story changes dependent on the state, not depending on what I choose to think.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.p: It can go the other way as well, especially with memories. It's tricky to discern, but sometimes when I'm working with someone who's grieving, they're just lost in their pain. So I'll ask a specific question: "When was the last time you hugged them, or smiled with them?" I'm trying to trigger the state through a story. As long as it clicks, they might smile and say, "Oh yeah, there was that one time..." I'm prompting a story, which then triggers the state.

And the state might bring up a story, like "What's the point of living without this person?", and that story reinforces the state. So it can become a self-perpetuating loop: story follows state follows story follows state.

I think that's why it's so helpful in therapy to say things out loud: to get it out of that loop and into somebody else's empathy, to receive co-regulation, and to allow the loop to break. It's similar to breaking a behavioral adaptation loop. Once the loop breaks, the person can move along the grieving path.

There's a lot to grief. It's been coming up way more in my therapy since COVID, with a lot of the kids and teenagers I work with grieving. With COVID, the loss was unexpected, there was panic surrounding it, and they were blocked from seeing their family member and saying goodbye in person. There are all these aspects that compound it.
